questions.q: Define a mixture and state the two main types. Give one example of each type from daily life.
questions.a: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances retaining their individual properties. The two main types are homogeneous (e.g., salt water) and heterogeneous (e.g., oil and water). A wrong answer (e.g., "mixture is a chemical combination" or "types are solid and liquid") reveals confusion between physical vs chemical combination and between states of matter vs mixture classification.

questions.q: Explain why a solution of copper sulphate in water is homogeneous while a mixture of chalk powder in water is heterogeneous. Use the concept of particle size in your answer.
questions.a: Copper sulphate dissolves as Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions (<1 nm), forming a single-phase uniform mixture. Chalk powder (CaCO₃) particles are >1000 nm, remain as separate solid phase, settle down, and make the mixture non-uniform. A wrong answer (e.g., "copper sulphate is blue so it's homogeneous") reveals reliance on color instead of particle size and phase uniformity as the defining criteria.

questions.q: You are given three beakers: A (milk), B (air), C (blood). Classify each as homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture. Justify each classification using particle size and phase behavior.
questions.a: A (milk): Heterogeneous (colloid) — fat globules ~100-1000 nm, shows Tyndall effect, separable by centrifugation. B (air): Homogeneous — gas molecules <1 nm, uniform composition, single phase. C (blood): Heterogeneous (colloid/suspension) — cells ~µm size, settles on standing, shows Tyndall effect. A wrong classification (e.g., "milk is homogeneous because it looks uniform") reveals the misconception that visual uniformity alone defines homogeneity, ignoring particle size and Tyndall effect.

questions.q: Compare the stability, filtration behavior, and Tyndall effect of a true solution (homogeneous) and a suspension (heterogeneous). Present your answer in a table.
questions.a:
| Property | True Solution (Homogeneous) | Suspension (Heterogeneous) |
|---|---|---|
| Stability | Stable, no settling | Unstable, particles settle |
| Filtration | Passes through filter paper | Residue left on filter paper |
| Tyndall Effect | Not shown | May show (if particles large enough to scatter) |
A wrong table (e.g., claiming solution shows Tyndall effect) reveals confusion between colloids and true solutions, and misunderstanding that Tyndall effect requires particles >40 nm.

questions.q: A student claims: "All transparent mixtures are homogeneous, and all opaque mixtures are heterogeneous." Evaluate this statement with two counterexamples.
questions.a: The statement is false. Counterexample 1: Milk is opaque but is a colloid (heterogeneous at microscopic level) — however, some colloids like gelatin can be transparent yet heterogeneous (particle size 1-1000 nm). Counterexample 2: Air is transparent and homogeneous; but a very dilute suspension of fine clay in water may appear slightly translucent yet is heterogeneous. A wrong evaluation (agreeing with the statement) reveals the misconception that optical transparency equals homogeneity, ignoring particle size criteria.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using only a flashlight, filter paper, and a stand to distinguish between three unknown mixtures: sugar solution, starch solution, and sand-water mixture. Write the procedure and expected observations.
questions.a: Procedure: 1) Shine flashlight through each mixture in a dark room — observe Tyndall effect. 2) Filter each mixture — observe residue. Expected: Sugar solution — no Tyndall effect, no residue (homogeneous). Starch solution — shows Tyndall effect (colloid), no residue (passes filter). Sand-water — may show Tyndall effect, sand residue on filter (heterogeneous suspension). A poor design (e.g., only testing filtration) reveals inability to use multiple properties (Tyndall + filtration) for complete classification.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A mixture is a material composed of two or more ______ (elements or compounds) physically combined in any proportion, where each substance retains its own chemical identity and properties.
Fill in the blank: Observe a glass of nimbu pani (______) and a glass of sand-water mixture side by side.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can classify a given mixture as homogeneous or heterogeneous by analyzing its composition uniformity, phase visibility, and particle size, and justify the classification using at least two distinguishing criteria (e.g., Tyndall effect, filtration behavior, stability).
